questions.question: Why is `{ status: "loading" } | { status: "success"; data: Fund[] } | { status: "error"; error: string }` usually better than `{ isLoading: boolean; error?: string; data?: Fund[] }`?
options: It makes impossible combinations, such as loading with an error and data, unrepresentable, and data is guaranteed present after checking status
It avoids the need for any runtime checks
Booleans are not allowed in strict mode
questions.explanation: Independent flags allow every combination, most of them nonsense, and force undefined checks everywhere. A discriminated union allows only the real states and narrows to the right shape after one tag check.

questions.question: In an exhaustive switch, the default branch calls `assertNever(p)` where `assertNever(x: never)`. A new union member is added but not handled. What happens?
options: The code compiles and silently returns undefined
assertNever is removed by the compiler
TypeScript reports an error because the unhandled member is not assignable to never
The new member is automatically handled by the first case
questions.explanation: After all handled cases are narrowed away, the remaining type should be never. An unhandled member remains, so passing it to a never parameter is a compile error that names the missing case.

questions.question: What does `Extract<Payment, { status: "draft" }>` give you when Payment is a discriminated union?
options: The union member whose status is "draft"
Every member except the draft one
A boolean indicating whether Payment has a draft state
questions.explanation: Extract keeps union members assignable to the given shape, which selects the draft member. You can then write functions such as submit(p: Draft) that reject payments in any other state.

questions.question: Given `type Result<T> = { ok: true; value: T } | { ok: false; error: string }`, when can a caller read `r.value`?
options: Always, because value is declared on the type
After checking that r.ok is true, which narrows r to the success member
questions.explanation: The boolean literal ok is the discriminant. Checking if (r.ok) narrows r to the member that has value; in the else branch only error is available.
